# 2026 Alachua County Voter Guide: County Commissioner, District 4

The upcoming general election on November 3, 2026, features a contest for the District 4 seat on the Alachua County Board of County Commissioners [1, 2]. The Board of County Commissioners is the primary legislative and policy-making body for Alachua County, Florida, holding authority over a budget that totals approximately $974 million, which includes a $327 million general operating fund, funding for the Sheriff's Office, Fire Rescue, animal resources, and local infrastructure [3, 4, 5]. 

Although commissioners are elected to occupy specific district seats, the 2026 election is conducted on an at-large basis, meaning all registered voters in Alachua County may cast a ballot in this race regardless of their specific geographic district [6, 7, 8]. The transition to an at-large voting system was finalized after a 2024 countywide referendum, which reversed a 2022 state-initiated measure that had temporarily instituted single-member district voting [8, 9, 10]. 

Because no candidates from the Republican Party or other political organizations qualified for the race by the June 2026 deadline, the contest bypassed the August primary and advanced directly to the November general election ballot [2, 11]. The two candidates appearing on the ballot are incumbent Ken Cornell, representing the Democratic Party, and challenger Dewayne Baines, running with No Party Affiliation (NPA) [1, 2]. 

## Ken Cornell (Democratic)

### 1. Background
Ken Cornell is a 57-year-old real estate professional and Certified Public Accountant (CPA) currently serving his third term as the Alachua County Commissioner for District 4 [2, 12]. Born and raised in Gainesville, Florida, Cornell attended local public schools, including Terwilliger Elementary, Ft. Clarke Middle School, and Buchholz High School [13]. He pursued higher education at the University of Florida, where he earned a master's degree with high honors from the Fisher School of Accounting [2, 13]. 

Professionally, Cornell operates as a trained CPA and holds the position of Broker-Associate and Senior Vice President with Bosshardt Realty Services, LLC [2, 13]. According to his official biography, his private-sector experience includes owning and operating several small businesses within Alachua County prior to entering public office [13]. 

Cornell's career in elected public service began in November 2014 when he was first elected to the Alachua County Commission [13]. He was subsequently re-elected without opposition in 2018 and won a third term in 2022 [13]. During the 2026 election cycle, Cornell bypassed the traditional financial qualifying fee by gathering 1,634 citizen petition signatures, meeting the statutory requirement of obtaining signatures from one percent of the total voters in the last election for the office [7]. Throughout his tenure on the commission, he has served multiple terms as the board's Chair, most recently being selected for the position by his fellow commissioners in November 2025 [14, 15]. 

Beyond his direct role on the county commission, Cornell’s public service record includes appointments to numerous civic and governmental advisory boards. Locally, he has served as the Chair of the Alachua County Children's Trust, a member of the Alachua County Library District Governing Board, and Chair of Career Source [12, 13]. He has also served on the Community Agency Partnership Program (CAPP) citizens advisory board and the Chamber of Commerce public policy board [13]. At the state and national levels, Cornell serves on the Board of Directors for the Florida Association of Counties (FAC) and was appointed to the FAC Finance and Audit Committee in June 2023 by the organization's president-elect, a role involving the review of the association's internal budgets and allocations [13, 16]. He is also a member of the National Association of Counties (NACo) Environment, Energy, and Land Use Steering Committee [13]. 

### 2. Stated Positions on the Major Issues
Cornell has outlined his policy priorities through his official campaign website, debate forums, and responses to local media and labor coalition questionnaires. His stated platform centers on continuing current county plans related to transportation infrastructure, fiscal management, affordable housing, and environmental conservation.

Regarding transportation and local infrastructure, Cornell states that maintaining the county's established ten-year transportation improvement plan is a primary objective. He points to his support for allocating over $250 million toward county road repairs and repaving over the next decade as evidence of this priority [12]. Furthermore, he asserts that his administration has facilitated investments in upgrading local stormwater systems to improve flood resilience [2]. 

On matters of fiscal policy and taxation, Cornell frequently references his accounting background, stating that financial discipline and maintaining strong budget reserves are central to his decision-making process [2, 7, 12]. He has publicly warned voters about the potential impacts of Amendment 3 (HJR 1-F), a state-level ballot initiative proposing an increase to the homestead tax exemption up to $250,000 by 2028. Cornell argues that if the amendment passes, it will reduce Alachua County's recurring revenue by over $80 million annually, requiring strict fiscal restraint from the commission [12]. He states that over his decade in office, he has repeatedly supported reducing the county's millage rate to the roll-back rate rather than capturing additional revenue from rising property values [12]. 

Cornell’s housing policy focuses on incentivizing the construction of affordable and workforce housing. He has advocated for utilizing tax-exempt bonds and property tax exemptions in coordination with private housing operators to redevelop specific county properties, a mechanism he argues minimizes financial risk to the county while expanding the housing supply [12, 17]. In response to a questionnaire from the Alachua County Labor Coalition (ACLC), Cornell stated his opposition to imposing work requirements and term limits on Section 8 housing voucher holders, citing data that suggests such rules create unnecessary barriers rather than addressing structural poverty [18]. 

On public transportation, Cornell informed the ACLC that the county must take a direct funding role in the Regional Transit System (RTS). He cited his previous push to restore weekend bus services to GRACE Marketplace and the local airport following funding cuts from the University of Florida [18]. Going forward, he advocates for the establishment of a dedicated, formula-based funding commitment across the university, the city, and the county to prevent budget shortfalls and to prioritize expanding fixed transit routes into unincorporated areas [18]. 

Regarding environmental protection and land use, Cornell states that he prioritizes the preservation of rural lands and water quality, advancing what he refers to as "circular economy strategies" to reduce waste and emissions [2, 19]. He maintains that development must pay for itself and should be heavily encouraged within the county's existing urban cluster to protect ecologically sensitive areas, such as the lakes in eastern Alachua County and the springs in the west [12]. 

### 3. Public Record
As a sitting commissioner for over eleven years, Cornell’s public record is extensively documented through his votes on the county budget, local ordinances, and board directives. 

During the September 2026 budget cycle, Cornell voted in favor of adopting the Fiscal Year 2027 (FY27) county budget, which outlined $974 million in total expenditures, including a $327 million general operating fund, $152 million for the Sheriff's Office, and $77 million for Fire Rescue [3, 4, 5]. Consistent with his stated fiscal platform, Cornell voted to adopt a roll-back general fund millage rate of 7.2107 mills, representing a decrease from the FY26 rate of 7.6000 mills, while maintaining the law enforcement Municipal Services Taxing Unit (MSTU) rate at 3.5678 mills [3, 4, 20]. 

Cornell's voting record demonstrates active involvement in the structure of the county's electoral system. Following a 2022 state-sponsored referendum that successfully transitioned Alachua County to single-member districts, Cornell publicly opposed the change, stating that at-large voting provides residents with a broader voice in county governance [6, 8]. In May 2024, Cornell introduced a successful motion to advertise a local ordinance placing the issue back before the voters [8, 21]. The subsequent November 2024 referendum, which returned the county to at-large districts, passed with 71% of the vote [9, 10]. Following the passage, Cornell stated that the result reaffirmed the voters' true preference after earlier confusion regarding the single-member system [9]. 

In May 2024, Cornell initiated a major shift in the county's financial portfolio by introducing a motion to eliminate all corporate investments from Alachua County's investment policy [8, 21]. The motion was introduced during a period of public comment wherein residents urged the county to issue a ceasefire resolution regarding the war in Gaza and to divest from the defense contractor Lockheed Martin [8]. Cornell's motion, which passed unanimously, restricted the county to investing solely in U.S. securities and principal-safe bonds, fully divesting the county from corporate stock holdings [21]. 

Additional documented decisions in Cornell's public record include his November 2025 vote to approve the county's comprehensive Climate Action Plan, an initiative he supported on the grounds that it would qualify the county for state funding to address local flooding issues [15]. He also voted to approve a controversial $2 million expenditure to install artificial intelligence-powered, in-facing dash cameras inside Alachua County fleet vehicles, an appropriation that drew criticism from residents who argued the funds should have been allocated to road repairs [12]. During a commission meeting concerning the paving of Totem Pole Road via a Special Assessment District, Cornell recused himself from the vote because he is an affected property owner in the district [22]. Furthermore, in media questionnaires, Cornell highlighted his vote against a county proposal to build and operate a local meat processing plant, a project he strongly opposed and which was ultimately canceled [12].

### 4. Campaign Funding
Official campaign finance reports filed with the Alachua County Supervisor of Elections in June 2026 indicate that Ken Cornell's campaign raised $107,000 [11]. 

An analysis of the top donor categories reveals that Cornell's campaign is primarily funded by local individual residents, regional business entities, and political action committees [23, 24]. Specific itemized contributors listed in state and county databases include individual donors such as Michael Dietz, Kathleen Barnes, and Virginia Seacrist, alongside corporate entities such as Farm Summershine [23]. State finance databases also document that Cornell made a personal contribution of $1,000 to a political committee titled "Alachua County's Future" [24].

### 5. Publicly Announced Endorsements
No verified information found. While Cornell completed candidate questionnaires for organizations such as the Alachua County Labor Coalition, no formal, publicly announced endorsements from advocacy groups, labor unions, or political action committees were documented in the available sources [18].

---

## Dewayne Baines (No Party Affiliation)

### 1. Background
Dewayne Baines is a 47-year-old social worker, community advocate, and Christian counselor running for the District 4 seat with no party affiliation [2, 11, 25, 26]. Like his opponent, Baines was born and raised in Gainesville, Florida [25, 26]. 

Baines's educational background includes an Associate of Arts degree in sociology from Santa Fe College, a Bachelor’s degree in Social Work from Saint Leo University, and a Master’s degree in Social Work (MSW) from the University of Louisville [25, 26, 27]. He also holds a degree in biotechnology [27]. 

Professionally, Baines operates in the fields of social services, vocational rehabilitation, and religious ministry. According to his professional resume and campaign biographies, he is the President and Founder of Youth Builder Faith Center INC, a position he has held since 2009, and the Founder of Jesus Christ Faith Center INC, which he established in 2007 [28]. His social work experience includes serving as an MSW intern at the Altrusa House of Gainesville in 2018 and 2019 [27, 28]. Additional documented professional experience includes working as an Educational Outreach Specialist and a vocational rehabilitation counselor in Raleigh, North Carolina, where he assisted youth and adults with career skills, strict-confidentiality crisis counseling, and community provider coordination [27]. He also has four years of experience serving as a youth basketball coach [25, 26].

Baines's prior public service is based on his appointments to local county advisory boards. In January 2021, the Alachua County Commission appointed Baines to a citizen-at-large position on the Alachua County Land Conservation Board [29]. The Land Conservation Board, established in 2000, is an eleven-member citizen advisory panel tasked with evaluating environmentally significant properties and recommending them to the County Commission for acquisition under the "Alachua County Forever" program [29]. Baines served a three-year term on this board [26, 27]. Additionally, his public records indicate a three-year term on the Alachua County Rural Concerns Advisory Committee, as well as prior service on a county disability advisory board over fifteen years ago [26, 27]. 

### 2. Stated Positions on the Major Issues
Baines communicates his policy positions primarily through his official campaign website and his responses to media questionnaires. His stated platform is largely focused on alleviating economic and infrastructure disparities, increasing affordable housing, and pursuing localized community development.

On the topic of economic and infrastructure disparities, Baines identified income inequality—specifically in East Gainesville—as one of the most pressing issues facing the county in a questionnaire submitted to News4JAX [2]. He stated that addressing these disparities requires community-focused strategies, and he proposed accelerating the county’s "Forward Focus" economic development plan [2]. According to Baines, this acceleration must involve increasing local job opportunities and directing essential services into East Gainesville to eliminate food deserts as defined by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) [2].

Regarding affordable and workforce housing, Baines states that he supports the direct utilization of the county's Affordable Housing Trust to fund transitional housing programs and direct financial assistance for residents [2]. He further proposes aligning county land-use policies with public-private partnerships to construct and increase the availability of permanent supportive housing for high-need populations [2]. On his official campaign website, he lists "Making affordable housing, affordable" as a central pillar of his platform [26]. 

In the area of environmental policy and climate resilience, Baines states his support for the full implementation of the county's Climate Action Plan [2]. He specifically proposed utilizing revenues generated by the Wild Spaces/Public Places Infrastructure Surtax to protect ecologically functional land corridors and to expand safe public recreation areas throughout the county [2]. His campaign website also lists a general commitment to policies that protect the local environment [25, 26].

On taxation and utilities, Baines lists specific economic goals on his campaign website aimed at lowering the cost of living for residents. These goals include "Making Property taxes affordable" and "Lowering Utility services," though specific mechanisms for achieving these reductions are not detailed in the available materials [25, 26]. 

Baines's broader governance platform includes generalized support for policies designed to keep local schools open, bolster small businesses, protect rural areas, and repair deteriorating road infrastructure [25, 26]. 

Unlike his opponent, Baines did not submit responses to comprehensive policy questionnaires sent by Mainstreet Daily News and the Alachua County Labor Coalition [12, 18]. Consequently, his specific stances on complex county issues such as the funding mechanisms for the Regional Transit System (RTS) and policies regarding Section 8 housing voucher requirements are not detailed in the public record [18].

### 3. Public Record
Because Baines has not previously held an elected executive or legislative office, his documented public record is strictly tied to his appointed service on Alachua County advisory panels, primarily the Alachua County Land Conservation Board from 2021 to 2024. 

Official county meeting minutes demonstrate that Baines regularly attended board sessions and participated in the evaluation of land parcels for conservation [29, 30, 31]. The record indicates that Baines engaged in making formal recommendations to the Board of County Commissioners regarding land acquisitions.
